meta.blurb: A driver takes a wrong turn in Sarajevo and stops near a young man with a gun. Within weeks, a promise from Berlin and a deadline for Serbia turn a crisis into a war much bigger than most leaders wanted.
meta.bible: This book follows the July Crisis of 1914, from 28 June to 4 August. Europe: the Great Powers, in two camps. The Triple Alliance: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy. France and Russia had an alliance from the 1890s; Britain had friendly understandings (Entente) with both. Archduke Franz Ferdinand: heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, shot with his wife Sophie in Sarajevo, Bosnia, on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb aged nineteen. Franz Joseph: the old emperor of Austria-Hungary. Vienna: its capital. Belgrade: the capital of Serbia. Berlin: Germany's capital. Kaiser Wilhelm: the German emperor. Bethmann Hollweg: the German Chancellor. Moltke: the German chief of staff. Schlieffen Plan: Germany's plan to beat France fast through Belgium, named after Alfred von Schlieffen, and its exact rigidity is debated by historians. Tsar Nicholas: the Russian emperor; St Petersburg: Russia's capital. Poincaré: the French president. Viviani: the French prime minister. Sir Edward Grey: the British foreign secretary. King Albert: the king of Belgium. Liège: Belgian fortress city. Treaty of London 1839: guaranteed Belgian neutrality. Key dates: 5 and 6 July Germany's blank cheque; 23 July Austria's ultimatum to Serbia (ten demands, forty-eight hours); 25 July Serbia's reply and Austria's partial mobilisation; 28 July Austria declares war on Serbia; 29 July partial Russian mobilisation, 30 July general order, 31 July in force; 31 July German ultimatums; 1 August Germany declares war on Russia and France mobilises; 2 August Germany's ultimatum to Belgium; 3 August Germany declares war on France; 4 August Germany invades Belgium and Britain declares war. Words: Ultimatum, Mobilisation, Mobilise, Mobilised, Mobilising, Reservists, Chancellor, Envoy, Frontier, Neutral, Neutrality, Ally, Allies, Alliance, Balkans, Slavs, Telegrams, Archduke, Empire, Empires, Cheque, Garrison. Voice: calm, clear and fair; the book shows that nobody planned the whole war and that historians still disagree about blame. No invented dates, numbers or quotes.

A1A2: In the summer of 1914, Europe looked calm, rich and full of life.
Europe's big countries had made promises to help their friends in a war.
Every big country had a huge army and a plan to move it by train.
Serbia was a small country, and its people dreamed of a bigger, stronger land.
On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand visited the city of Sarajevo.
That morning a young man threw a bomb at his car, but it missed.
Later the car stopped near Gavrilo Princip, who shot the archduke and his wife.
The news shocked Europe, and Austria wanted to punish Serbia for the killings.
Austria wanted war with Serbia, but it was afraid of big Russia.
So Austria sent a letter to Germany and asked for its help.
On 5 July, the German Kaiser promised to stand with Austria, whatever happened.
German leaders feared Russia was growing stronger, so they did not want to wait.
For many weeks, Europe heard nothing, and many leaders went on holiday.
On 23 July, Austria sent Serbia a hard message with a short time limit.
Serbia had to stop groups against Austria, and let Austrian officials work there.
Serbia said yes to most of the demands, but not to all of them.
Austria's ambassador left Belgrade that night, and both countries began to prepare their armies.
Britain asked the big countries to meet and talk, but Germany said no.
The Kaiser read Serbia's answer and said there was no reason for war.
Austria declared war on Serbia on 28 July, and its guns fired on Belgrade.
Russia did not want to let Serbia fall, so the Tsar was worried.
Russia began to call up its soldiers, first some of them and then all.
Calling up an army and sending it to the border takes many days.
The Kaiser and the Tsar were related, and they sent messages asking for peace.
Germany had a plan to beat France fast and then turn to Russia.
On 31 July, Germany told Russia to stop calling up its army within twelve hours.
Germany asked France to stay out of the war and gave it eighteen hours.
France moved its soldiers back from the border to show it wanted peace.
On 1 August, Germany declared war on Russia, and France called up its army.
The Kaiser wanted to fight only Russia, but his general said that was impossible.
Britain had not promised to fight, and its leaders did not agree about war.
Britain had promised long ago to protect Belgium, a small and neutral country.
On 2 August, Germany asked Belgium to let its army pass, but Belgium said no.
On 3 August, Germany declared war on France.
On 4 August, German soldiers crossed the border into Belgium.
Britain told Germany to stop, and gave it until midnight.
Germany did not answer, so Britain was at war with Germany that night.
In many cities, crowds sang and cheered, but others were afraid.
Italy stayed out at first, and later other countries joined the war.
People still argue about who was most to blame for the war.
Austria wanted a short, hard war, and it did not think about the cost.
Germany gave Austria its full support, and then made a plan that had no pause.
Russia, France and Britain also made choices that made the war more likely.
In those days, leaders did not have time, trust or a way to stop.
Most people thought the war would be short, but it was not.
The war lasted more than four years, and millions of people died.
By the end, four old empires had fallen, and the map of Europe changed.
One lesson is to slow down, and to keep talking when you are afraid.
Another lesson is to ask what the other side fears, not only what it wants.
In thirty days, the choices of a few people led millions into war.
B1B2: In the summer of 1914, Europe seemed peaceful and prosperous. Yet beneath the calm, the great powers had been arming for years and trusted each other very little.
Germany and Austria-Hungary were allies, and so were France and Russia. Britain was friendly with France and Russia, but it had not promised to fight for either.
Every great power had millions of men who could be called up as soldiers. Each one also had a detailed plan for moving them to the border by train.
Serbia was a small country in the Balkans, and many Serbs dreamed of uniting all their people. Austria-Hungary, its large neighbour, ruled Bosnia, where many Serbs lived.

On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, visited Sarajevo with his wife Sophie. Some people in the crowd had come to cheer, but a few young men had come with other plans.
The first attacker threw a bomb at the archduke's car, but it bounced off and exploded under the car behind. Several people were hurt, though the archduke and Sophie were not.
On the way to visit the injured in hospital, the driver took a wrong turn. When the car stopped to reverse, Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb of nineteen, stepped forward and fired.

The news shocked the whole of Europe, and in Vienna it was seen as an attack on the empire. Princip and his friends were arrested, and Austria-Hungary soon learned that their weapons had come from Serbia.
Many leaders in Vienna wanted to crush Serbia once and for all. They feared, however, that Russia would come to Serbia's help.
So Austria sent an envoy to Berlin with a personal letter from its emperor. The letter asked whether Germany would stand beside Austria if Russia joined in.

On 5 and 6 July, Kaiser Wilhelm and his chancellor promised Germany's full support, whatever Austria decided to do. Later this was called a blank cheque, because Austria could fill in any amount it liked.
German leaders believed that Russia was growing stronger every year. They hoped the quarrel would stay small, but they were ready to accept the risk of a big war.
Austria did not act at once, because its leaders argued among themselves and many soldiers were at home for the harvest. Meanwhile, the French president sailed to Russia on a planned visit.
On the evening of 23 July, Austria delivered an ultimatum to Serbia. An ultimatum is a final demand with a deadline, and this one gave Serbia just forty-eight hours.

Serbia was told to ban groups and newspapers that were hostile to Austria, and to dismiss officials whom Austria named. It was also told to let Austrian officials help with the investigation inside Serbia.

Serbia replied just before the deadline and accepted most of the demands. It refused the one that would let Austrian officials work inside Serbia, and it offered to take the dispute to an international court.
Austria's ambassador left Belgrade by train that same evening. Serbia, which had already ordered its army to mobilise, now expected war.

In London, the foreign secretary, Sir Edward Grey, proposed a meeting of the four great powers that were not directly involved. Germany refused, saying it would not call its ally before a court of other nations.

On the morning of 28 July, Kaiser Wilhelm read Serbia's reply and wrote that every reason for war had disappeared. He suggested that Austria occupy Belgrade and then stop, but his advice arrived too late to change events.
On 28 July, exactly a month after the murder, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. The next day its guns, firing from across the river, began to bombard Belgrade.
Tsar Nicholas did not want war, but Russia thought of itself as the protector of the Serbs. If he stood by, he feared that Russia would lose its place as a great power in the Balkans.
On 29 July, Russia ordered a partial mobilisation against Austria. The next day the Tsar agreed to a full one, because his generals said that a partial plan could not work.
Mobilisation meant calling up millions of reservists and sending them to the frontier by train. It could not be paused halfway without chaos, and neighbours could see the trains begin to move.

Kaiser Wilhelm and Tsar Nicholas were related, and they sent each other telegrams in English, signed Willy and Nicky. Each asked the other to keep the peace, but neither could stop the plans that were already moving.

Germany feared a war on two fronts, against France in the west and Russia in the east. Its plan, named after General Schlieffen, was to beat France in a few weeks by marching through Belgium, and then to turn east.
On 31 July, Germany declared a state of imminent danger of war and sent an ultimatum to Russia. It demanded that Russia stop its mobilisation within twelve hours.
Germany also asked France whether it would stay neutral if Germany and Russia went to war. It gave France eighteen hours, and France replied that it would act as its own interests required.

To show that it wanted peace, France ordered its troops to stay ten kilometres from the border. Even so, on 1 August, France ordered mobilisation, because Russia and Germany were already preparing their armies.
On the evening of 1 August, Germany declared war on Russia. By then the armies of the great powers were on the move.
That evening the Kaiser asked whether the army could march against Russia alone. His chief of staff, Moltke, answered that the great plan for the march west could not be changed in a day.
Britain had no alliance that forced it to fight, and its government was divided. Many ministers wanted to stay out, while others thought Britain could not let France be crushed.
A treaty from 1839 had been signed by Britain, France, Russia, Austria and Prussia to guarantee that Belgium would always stay neutral. This promise would soon matter more than any alliance.
On the evening of 2 August, Germany asked Belgium to let its army cross the country, and gave twelve hours to answer. Belgium's king and government refused, even though their army was small.
On 3 August, Germany declared war on France, claiming that French aircraft had bombed German cities. This claim was false, and it is remembered as an excuse rather than a reason.
On 4 August, German soldiers crossed the frontier into Belgium. The small Belgian army fought to hold the fortress city of Liège, and it slowed the Germans for some days.
That day Britain sent Germany an ultimatum, demanding a promise to respect Belgium. The deadline was midnight in Berlin, which was eleven o'clock in London.
No answer came from Germany, and the deadline passed. Britain was at war, and lands of its empire, including Canada, Australia and India, were drawn in too.
In Berlin, Paris, London and Vienna, large crowds cheered and sang as the war began. Historians say, however, that many people were quietly afraid.
Italy, although it was Germany's ally on paper, declared itself neutral. Others joined later, including Japan, the Ottoman Empire and, in 1915, Italy on the opposite side.
People have argued for a century about who was most to blame. After 1919, the peace treaty said that Germany and its allies were responsible, but many historians now describe a more shared story.

Austria-Hungary wanted a short, sharp war against Serbia, and it set the crisis in motion. Its leaders knew that Russia might step in, and they went ahead because they trusted Germany to hold Russia back.
Germany gave Austria its full support without asking about its plans. Then it relied on a military plan that left almost no room for delay or talks.
Russia's mobilisation alarmed Germany, and France had promised to stand by Russia. Britain, meanwhile, did not make clear until the last days what it would do.
Leaders had little time to think, little trust in each other, and no easy way to pause. Each country feared being the last to prepare, so each moved a little earlier than it wished.
Most people expected a short war, and many soldiers believed they would be home within months. They were wrong, because new weapons such as machine guns made defending easier than attacking.
The war lasted more than four years, from 1914 to 1918. Close to ten million soldiers died in it, and the exact number is uncertain, while millions of civilians suffered as well.
By 1922, four great empires had disappeared: the German, the Austro-Hungarian, the Russian and the Ottoman. New countries appeared on the map, and new quarrels began.
One lesson of 1914 is that leaders should slow down in a crisis. If they are afraid, they should keep talking and keep their options open for as long as they can.
Another lesson is to ask what the other side fears, not only what it wants. Many steps taken in 1914 were meant as defence, but they looked like preparations for attack.

It took thirty days, from Germany's promise on 5 July to Britain's declaration on 4 August, for a regional crisis to become a world war. No single person wanted that result, yet choices made one after another led millions into it.
C1C2: In the summer of 1914, Europe looked like the safest and most prosperous place on Earth, with busy cities, fast new railways and holidaymakers crowding every beach. Yet beneath that calm, the great powers had spent years building armies and quietly planning for a war that all of them claimed not to want. In little more than a month, one murder in a small city would drag almost every one of them into it.

By 1914, Europe had divided itself into two armed camps, each held together by solemn promises of help. Germany and Austria-Hungary stood on one side, while France and Russia, who had signed an alliance of their own in the 1890s, stood on the other. Britain, although it had grown close to the French and the Russians, had signed no promise to fight for either.

Every great power kept a huge army that could be called up in a matter of days, and every general staff had prepared a precise railway timetable for sending its soldiers to the frontier. These plans were drawn up in peacetime, in quiet offices, by officers who believed that the side that moved first would win. Few of them had thought hard about how to stop once the trains began to run.

In the Balkans, the small kingdom of Serbia dreamed of uniting the Serbs who lived beyond its borders. Austria-Hungary, a sprawling empire of many peoples, had taken over Bosnia in 1878 and formally annexed it in 1908, and it saw Serbian ambition as a threat to its own survival. Russia, which felt close to the Serbs as fellow Slavs, watched the quarrel with growing concern.

On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, who was next in line to the throne of Austria-Hungary, drove through the streets of Sarajevo in an open car beside his wife Sophie. Crowds lined the road to watch the royal visitors pass, and many waved small flags as the cars rolled slowly by. Hidden among them stood several young men, all of them armed, who believed that their land should be free of Austrian rule.

The first of the young men threw a bomb at the royal car, but it bounced off the folded roof and exploded beneath the vehicle behind. Several people were injured, though the archduke and his wife were unhurt, and the car sped on to the town hall. Most of the other plotters, confused by the speed of events, lost their chance.

On the way to the hospital to visit the injured, the driver took a wrong turn and halted the car to reverse, only a few steps from where Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb of nineteen, happened to be standing. He stepped forward and fired twice at close range, and both bullets found their targets. Within minutes, both the archduke and his wife Sophie had died of their wounds.

The murders shocked Europe, and in Vienna they were treated as an attack on the empire itself. The young men were quickly arrested, and investigators found that their bombs and pistols had come from Serbia, with the help of some Serbian officers. Historians still argue about how much the Serbian government knew, but Austrian leaders were in no mood to wait for the answer.

Austria's generals and ministers saw a chance to deal with Serbia once and for all, and the old emperor, Franz Joseph, who was eighty-three, agreed that the Serbs must be dealt with firmly. But they knew that an attack on Serbia might bring the huge Russian army down on them. Without a strong friend at their side, they felt that they dared not move against Serbia at all.

Fearing Russia, Vienna sent an envoy to Berlin carrying a personal letter from the old emperor to the German Kaiser. The letter explained that Serbia must be dealt with by force, and it asked a question on which everything would depend. Would Germany stand firmly beside its ally if Russia decided to come to the defence of Serbia?

On 5 and 6 July, Kaiser Wilhelm and his chancellor, Bethmann Hollweg, told the Austrians that Germany would support them fully, whatever they chose to do. Historians later called this promise a blank cheque, because Austria was free to fill in any amount it liked. From these two days it was about thirty days to the moment when Britain, too, would be at war.

Many German leaders believed that Russia was growing stronger with every year, and some felt that if a war must come, it was better to fight it soon. They hoped that Russia would stand aside, and that the quarrel between Austria and Serbia would stay small. Yet they were prepared to accept a larger war rather than see their only reliable ally humbled.

For almost four weeks after the murder, Vienna said nothing, and across Europe people began to hope that the crisis would fade. In fact Austria was drafting a demand for Serbia that was harsh enough for many historians to believe it hoped for a refusal. It chose to deliver it only after the French president, Raymond Poincaré, had finished a state visit to Russia.

At six o'clock on the evening of 23 July, an Austrian diplomat in Belgrade handed the Serbian government an ultimatum, which is a final demand backed by a threat. It listed ten demands and gave Serbia just forty-eight hours to accept all of them. Almost everyone who read it in the capitals of Europe understood that it was meant to be hard to accept.

Serbia was ordered to ban newspapers and groups that spoke against Austria-Hungary, to dismiss any officials whom Vienna chose to name, and to punish those involved in the plot. Among the demands that troubled Belgrade most was one that would allow Austrian officials to take part in the investigation on Serbian soil. Serbian leaders feared that this would make their country an Austrian puppet in all but name.

Serbia answered a few minutes before the deadline on 25 July, and its reply was so polite and so full of concessions that many observers across Europe were astonished. It accepted most of the demands, at least in part, but it refused to let Austrian officials work inside its own borders and offered to put the dispute before an international court. Austria's ambassador, who had orders to leave unless every demand was met, judged the answer insufficient after a brief look.

Within half an hour, Austria's ambassador had packed his bags and boarded a train out of Belgrade, and diplomatic relations between the two countries were broken. Serbia, which had already begun calling up its army, expected invasion at any moment. Austria, for its part, ordered a partial mobilisation of its own army, aimed at Serbia alone.

In London, the foreign secretary, Sir Edward Grey, proposed that Britain, Germany, France and Italy should meet to find a peaceful solution, since none of them was directly involved in the quarrel. France and Italy agreed, and so did Russia, but the Germans refused, saying that they would not drag Austria before a court of other nations. A chance to slow the crisis and give the diplomats time to work was lost.

On the morning of 28 July, Kaiser Wilhelm read Serbia's reply in full for the first time and wrote on it that every reason for war had disappeared. He suggested that Austria occupy Belgrade and then halt, holding the city as a pledge while talks went on. By then, however, events were moving too fast, and Austria declared war that same day.

On 28 July, a month to the day after the murder in Sarajevo, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. The following day, Austrian guns and river gunboats began to bombard Belgrade across the water. A quarrel between two countries had become a war, and everyone waited to see who else would join.

Tsar Nicholas was a man who hoped to avoid a war, but his ministers and generals insisted that Russia could not abandon Serbia. If Russia stood aside while Austria crushed the Serbs, they argued, it would lose its influence in the Balkans and its standing as a great power. The Tsar was therefore caught between his wish for peace and the pressure of those around him.

On 29 July, Russia ordered a partial mobilisation aimed only at Austria-Hungary, hoping to frighten Vienna without alarming Berlin. Russia's generals, however, told the Tsar that such a limited plan would ruin the arrangements for a full one, and on 30 July he agreed to mobilise the whole army. The order took effect on 31 July, and the news travelled across the continent within hours.

Mobilisation meant calling up millions of reservists, collecting horses, guns and supplies, and sending them all to the frontier by train. Once begun it was extremely hard to stop, because halting halfway would create chaos and leave the country defenceless. To the neighbours who watched the trains begin to move, mobilisation therefore looked a great deal like the first step of an attack.

Kaiser Wilhelm and Tsar Nicholas were related, and in those last days they exchanged a stream of telegrams in English, signed with their nicknames, Willy and Nicky. Each begged the other to avoid war, and both seem to have meant it. Yet neither man could hold back the generals and the timetables, and the messages were overtaken by events.

Germany's greatest fear was a war on two fronts, with France in the west and Russia in the east. The famous plan, named after the former chief of staff Alfred von Schlieffen, called for a lightning victory over France by sweeping through Belgium, after which the army would turn east by train to face the slower Russians. Historians still debate how rigid the plan really was, but the generals of 1914 felt that they had no other workable one.

On 31 July, Germany proclaimed a state of imminent danger of war, and its ambassador in St Petersburg was ordered to deliver an ultimatum. Russia was to stop every preparation against Germany and Austria within twelve hours, or Germany would mobilise in turn. No answer came, because the Tsar's government believed that it could not safely undo what it had begun.

On the same day, Germany asked France whether it would stay neutral in a war between Germany and Russia, and gave it only eighteen hours to answer. The question was hardly sincere, because France had an alliance with Russia and the Germans knew it. The French prime minister replied that France would do what its own interests demanded.

On 30 July, the French government ordered its troops to stay ten kilometres back from the frontier, so that no clash could be blamed on France or used as an excuse for war. It was a striking gesture of good faith, but the pressure of events meant that it could not last. On 1 August, with Russia mobilising and Germany preparing to do the same, France ordered mobilisation of its own.

On the evening of 1 August, Germany, having received no answer to its ultimatum, declared war on Russia. By then the armies of Germany, Russia, France and Austria-Hungary were all either on the move or about to be. Crowds gathered in the squares of Berlin to hear the news, and many people sang.

Late that evening, the Kaiser, who had received a confused report that Britain might stay neutral if France was left alone, asked whether the whole army might march east instead. His chief of staff, Helmuth von Moltke, answered that this was impossible, because the deployment had been planned for years and could not be improvised in a day. The most powerful man in Germany had learned that he could not easily steer the machine he was supposed to command.

In London, the cabinet was bitterly divided, for Britain had no treaty that forced it to fight and many ministers, as well as much of the public, wanted to stay out. Others argued that if Germany crushed France and Russia, it would dominate the whole continent. Sir Edward Grey had also promised the French that the British navy would protect their northern coast, which was hard to square with standing aside.

An old treaty, signed in 1839 by Britain, France, Russia, Austria and Prussia, had guaranteed that Belgium would stay neutral and free from attack. Prussia had since become the heart of the German Empire, so Germany inherited the promise. It was an obscure document to most people, but it was about to matter more than any alliance.

On the evening of 2 August, Germany demanded that Belgium allow its army to cross the country, promising to pay for any damage and threatening to treat a refusal as hostile. King Albert and his ministers met through the night in the capital, with only twelve hours in which to answer. Although Belgium's army was small, they decided to refuse, and the reply was sent the next morning.

On 3 August, Germany declared war on France, claiming that French aircraft had bombed German cities. These claims were untrue, and historians regard them as an excuse rather than a reason. The real motive was the plan, which demanded that the army strike France without delay.

On the morning of 4 August, German soldiers crossed the frontier into Belgium and marched towards the fortress city of Liège. The small Belgian army fought hard, and the forts around the city held out for days longer than the German staff had expected. The invasion that was meant to win the war quickly had begun with a delay.

Britain, now certain where Germany was marching, sent Berlin an ultimatum on 4 August demanding a promise that Belgium would be left alone. The deadline was midnight in Berlin, which was eleven o'clock in the evening in London. In the streets near Downing Street, people waited in the summer dusk for news.

No satisfactory answer came from Berlin, and when the deadline passed, Britain was at war with Germany. Because the dominions of the British Empire had no separate foreign policy at that time, lands as far apart as Canada, Australia and India were drawn in as well. It was exactly thirty days since the Kaiser had promised Austria his support, and in that time a local crisis had grown into a continental war.

In Berlin, Paris, London and Vienna, crowds gathered to cheer and sing, and soldiers leaving for the stations were showered with flowers. Historians now think the mood was more mixed than these famous scenes suggest, for many families, particularly in the countryside, received the news with dread. Both the joy and the fear were real, and few people imagined how long the war would last.

Italy, though it belonged to the same alliance as Germany and Austria-Hungary, declared that the treaty did not oblige it to fight and stayed neutral. Japan entered the war against Germany later in August, and the Ottoman Empire joined the German side in the autumn. In 1915, after bargaining with both sides, Italy itself changed camps and went to war against Austria-Hungary.

For more than a century, people have argued about who was most to blame for the war. The peace treaty of 1919 placed the responsibility on Germany and its allies, but many historians today describe a shared failure in which leaders in several capitals took risks they did not fully understand. The debate has never ended, because each new set of documents adds something to the picture.

Austria-Hungary's leaders wanted to punish Serbia and to end its influence in the Balkans, and it was they who turned a murder into a crisis. They knew that Russia might step in, but they trusted Germany to restrain it, and they delayed so long that much of the early sympathy for Austria faded. Their aim was a small, sharp war, yet their decisions made a very large one possible.

Germany gave Austria its full support without insisting on knowing what Vienna intended to do. Once the crisis spread, German leaders were bound by a military plan that left almost no room for delay or negotiation, because the army believed it had to strike France within days. The decision to invade a neutral Belgium, taken because the plan required it, also brought Britain into the war.

Russia mobilised its vast army before Germany had done so, which alarmed Berlin, and France had assured its ally that it would stand beside it. Many historians also think that Serbia could have done more to restrain the extremists whose weapons came from its territory. Britain's leaders, meanwhile, left Germany unsure until the last days about whether they would fight, and this uncertainty may have weakened the chance of deterring it.

What the leaders lacked, above all, was time, trust and a way to pause. Each government feared that waiting would give its enemies an advantage, and each therefore moved a little earlier than it wished, which in turn frightened its neighbours. In such a spiral, even people who truly wanted peace found themselves taking steps that made peace harder to keep.

Almost everyone expected a short war, and many soldiers left for the front believing that they would be home within months. They had not reckoned with machine guns, rapid-firing artillery and barbed wire, which favoured the defender so heavily that armies soon dug themselves into long lines of trenches. The quick victory that every general's plan had promised never came, and the war settled into a long, grinding struggle.

The war lasted more than four years and ended in November 1918, and by then close to ten million soldiers had died, with the exact total uncertain. Millions of civilians also lost their lives, to hunger, to disease and to the hardships of occupation and war. Whole towns had been destroyed, and almost every family in Europe knew someone who would never come home.

By 1922, four great empires had vanished: the German, the Austro-Hungarian, the Russian and the Ottoman. In their place stood new republics and new nations, some of them hopeful and some of them bitter about the borders they had been given. The settlement that followed the war solved some old problems, but it also left others that would trouble the century to come.

One lesson of 1914 is the value of slowness, and of patience, when a crisis begins to gather speed. Leaders who keep talking, who allow time for messages to be answered and tempers to cool, and who avoid tying themselves to plans that cannot be stopped, give peace its best chance. In 1914 the opposite happened, and the pace of events was set by timetables rather than by judgment.

Another lesson is to ask what the other side fears, and not merely what it wants. Many of the steps taken in 1914 were intended as defence, such as mobilising an army or marching through a neighbour's land, but they looked like preparations for attack to those who watched. A leader who cannot imagine how his actions appear to others is easily surprised by the reply.

It took thirty days, from Germany's promise to Austria on 5 July to Britain's declaration of war on 4 August, for a quarrel in the Balkans to become a war that spanned the world. Nobody planned it that way, and nobody seems to have wanted that outcome, yet each decision, taken by tired people in rooms far from the front, made the next one harder to refuse. That is the lasting warning of these thirty days: wars can arrive not through one great blunder but through many small steps.
